summary: Best current practices for third party call control in SIP, where one party sets up a call in which the communication is actually between other parties. SIP allows several approaches, each with trade-offs, and this document discusses which are good to use. It is a best current practice, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Third-party call control lets one SIP controller set up a call between two other parties. RFC 3725 compares four call flows and recommends different flows depending on whether the called party is a person or an endpoint that answers immediately.

subtitle: Recommended SIP call flows for connecting two parties through a third-party controller.

tldr.problem: A SIP controller can establish a call between two other parties in several ways, and the flows differ in complexity, timing and failure behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes four message flows and recommends Flow IV for people or unknown parties, Flow I for an endpoint that answers immediately, and avoiding Flow II.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Best Current Practice for third-party call control, not a new protocol. It also discusses failures, early media, preconditions and security.

today: RFC 3725 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 85) published in April 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Third-Party Call Control Does
sections.content:
Third-party call control (3pcc) lets a controller create and manage a communication session between other parties. In SIP, the controller is a user agent that wants to establish a session between two other user agents.

The RFC describes uses such as operator services, conferencing and click-to-dial. The participants exchange media directly; the controller coordinates their SIP signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller arranges a call between two other parties. It manages the setup messages, while the participants exchange the media.

sections.title: Four Ways to Establish the Call
sections.content:
Flow I asks party A for an offer, passes it to B, then returns B's answer to A. It is simple and needs no SDP manipulation, but it works best when B will answer immediately because A waits for an acknowledgment.

Flow II starts with a black-hole SDP offer and uses re-INVITEs. The controller must know the media types in advance, and repeated SDP changes can create an endless re-INVITE loop. Flow III avoids guessing the media but requires the controller to alter SDP. Flow IV starts with SDP containing no media lines, then passes the later offer and answer between A and B with only an origin-line change.
sections.plainLanguage: Each flow differs in when it sends session details and how much the controller must change them. Flow IV avoids most SDP editing but alerts party A before media is ready.

sections.title: Which Flow to Use
sections.content:
The RFC says Flow I SHOULD be used when the controller knows B is an automaton that will answer immediately, such as a media or conferencing server. For calls to people or unknown parties, Flow IV is RECOMMENDED. Flow III MAY be used, though the RFC says it offers no extra benefit over Flow IV.

Flow II SHOULD NOT be used because of its potential for an endless sequence of re-INVITEs. Flow IV has a trade-off: A may be alerted before the controller knows whether the parties share compatible media.
sections.plainLanguage: Use Flow I when the other endpoint is known to answer immediately. Use Flow IV for people or unknown endpoints, and avoid Flow II because its re-INVITEs can loop.

sections.title: Handling Call Failures
sections.content:
If the attempt to contact B fails, the RFC recommends that the controller send a BYE to A. The BYE should include a Reason header with the failure response so A can present the reason, such as a busy signal.

If A sends a re-INVITE while the controller is waiting for B's response, the controller cannot forward it as another INVITE transaction is already pending. A 491 response is recommended; A may retry after the pending exchange finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: If B cannot join, the controller tells A why the call failed. If A asks for a change while another request is pending, the controller can ask A to try again.

sections.title: Early Media and Preconditions
sections.content:
Early media is session data exchanged before a call is accepted, often tones or announcements. The RFC adapts Flow IV to pass early media from either participant. When A has not answered, the controller uses UPDATE rather than re-INVITE to pass session details.

Preconditions can tie call alerting to resource reservation. A controller can use them so participants are not alerted until compatible media is available and required reservations are made. A controller that does not handle preconditions specifically can pass the related session descriptions between the parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Early media lets callers hear tones or announcements before the call is accepted. Preconditions can delay alerting until both sides have the required media resources.

sections.title: Identity and Media Security
sections.content:
Third-party calls must continue to follow normal SIP authorization policies. The controller should identify the user requesting the call and authenticate itself as that user or as the party it represents.

SIP message protection is between each participant and the controller because the controller is part of both dialogs. Media keys can still protect media between the participants, but the RFC notes that the controller could interfere with the initial key exchange and insert itself into the media path.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller must show who asked it to make the call. Media can be protected between the participants, but that depends on the controller not altering their key exchange.
